title: The Blue Lunch Box
description: A new colleague finds a simple way to start a conversation at lunch.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: The Blue Lunch Box
units.contentMarkdown:
It is twelve o'clock. Lina is in the kitchen at work. Her lunch is in a blue box. She has rice, chicken and a small tomato.

A man comes into the kitchen. He has a blue box too.

"Hello. Is this your lunch?" he asks.

Lina looks at his box. There is a white star on it.

"No. My box has my name on it. Look: Lina."

"I'm Adam. This is my first day. Where can I sit?"

"Here. This chair is free."

Adam opens his box. He has bread, cheese and an apple.

"There is hot water over there," Lina says. "Do you want tea?"

"Yes, please. Where are the cups?"

"In the cupboard, next to the window."

They sit at the small table. Adam asks about the office. Lina asks about his family. Lunch is only twenty minutes, but Adam now knows one person at work.

Before they leave, he writes his name on his box.

title: Two Tickets, Please
description: Two visitors ask for bus tickets and check the way to a park.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: Two Tickets, Please
units.contentMarkdown:
Maya and her brother Sami are at a bus station. They want to visit Green Park. Maya speaks to the woman at the ticket desk.

Maya: Hello. Two tickets to Green Park, please.

Woman: Single tickets or return tickets?

Maya: Sorry. What is a return ticket?

Woman: You can go to the park and come back with it.

Maya: Return tickets, please. How much are they?

Woman: Six pounds for two people.

Maya: Can I pay by card?

Woman: Yes. Put your card here.

Sami: Is the bus outside?

Woman: Yes, but that's the bus to the airport. Your bus is number eight. It stops across the road.

Maya: Number eight. Thank you. What time is the next bus?

Woman: At ten fifteen. In five minutes.

Sami: Does it stop near the park entrance?

Woman: Yes. The stop is next to a flower shop.

Maya: Great. Thank you for your help.

They cross the road at the lights. Sami checks the number before they get on.

title: A Quiet Place for Tea
description: Neighbours agree on a comfortable time and place to meet.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: A Quiet Place for Tea
units.contentMarkdown:
Noor lives in a small flat. Her neighbour Eva lives upstairs. They say hello on the stairs, but they do not often talk.

On Saturday, Eva sees Noor with a bag of oranges.

"Those look nice," she says.

"They are for my sister. She is here today. Do you want to come for tea?"

"Thank you. What time?"

"Is four o'clock good?"

"I work until four. Is five OK?"

"Yes. Come at five."

At five, Eva knocks on Noor's door. She has some biscuits.

"Come in," says Noor. "This is my sister, Amal."

The kitchen is warm. A small child is asleep in the next room, so they speak quietly. Eva puts the biscuits on a plate. Amal makes tea.

They talk about the street and the shops near their homes. Eva knows a good place for fresh bread.

"Let's go there tomorrow," says Noor.

"In the morning?"

"Yes. After breakfast."

Eva smiles. Now she has someone to go with.

title: No Onions in My Sandwich
description: A customer asks about a sandwich and checks an order politely.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: No Onions in My Sandwich
units.contentMarkdown:
Ben is at a small café. He has ten minutes before his English class. He looks at the menu above the counter.

Ben: Hello. Can I have a cheese sandwich, please?

Server: Of course. With tomato and onion?

Ben: With tomato, please, but no onions.

Server: No onions. Anything to drink?

Ben: A small coffee with milk, please.

Server: Is that to eat here or take away?

Ben: To take away. My class starts soon.

Server: That's five pounds fifty.

Ben pays and waits by the window. The server puts a bag on the counter.

Server: Cheese sandwich and a small coffee.

Ben: Thank you. Sorry, is this my sandwich? There are onions in it.

Server: Oh, I'm sorry. That's another customer's order. Your sandwich is here. Tomato, no onions.

Ben: That's right. Thank you.

Server: Here's your coffee. Be careful. It's hot.

Outside, Ben checks his bag. He has his sandwich, a napkin and a spoon. His classroom is just across the street.

title: The Wrong Platform
description: A traveller deals with a platform change without missing her train.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: The Wrong Platform
units.contentMarkdown:
When Hana arrived at the station, the screen said that her train left from platform three. She bought a bottle of water and walked there with her suitcase. She was visiting a friend in another city for the weekend.

Ten minutes later, a message came from the loudspeaker. Hana heard the name of her destination, but she couldn't understand the rest. People around her started moving.

She showed her ticket to a station worker.

"Excuse me. Is this the right platform for my train?"

"Not now. There's a platform change. You need platform six."

"Do I have to go up the stairs? My suitcase is quite heavy."

"You can take the lift. It's behind you, next to the newsagent's. Go up one floor, then follow the signs."

Hana thanked him and checked the time. She still had twelve minutes. At the lift, an older woman was looking at the same ticket.

"Are you going to platform six too?" Hana asked.

The woman nodded. They travelled up together and found the platform without running. Their train was already there, but the doors were open.

After Hana found her seat, she sent her friend a message: "I'm on the train. Small adventure at the station!"

Then she put her suitcase away. Next time, she decided, she would check the screen again just before getting on.

title: Can We Move the Meeting?
description: Colleagues rearrange a meeting and make the new plan clear.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: Can We Move the Meeting?
units.contentMarkdown:
Daniel works in a small design office. On Tuesday morning, he calls his colleague Aisha. They have a meeting with a client at two o'clock.

Daniel: Hi, Aisha. Have you got a minute?

Aisha: Yes. What's the matter?

Daniel: The client just called. Her train is late. She can't get here before three.

Aisha: I have another meeting at three thirty. Could we meet online tomorrow morning instead?

Daniel: She wants to see the paper samples, so she needs to come to the office.

Aisha: Right. How about Thursday at ten?

Daniel: I'm visiting our supplier then. I'm free after lunch, though.

Aisha: Thursday at one thirty works for me. We can use the small meeting room.

Daniel: Shall I call her and ask?

Aisha: Yes, please. And don't cancel today's meeting in the calendar until she agrees.

Twenty minutes later, Daniel calls again.

Daniel: Thursday is fine. She asked how long the meeting will take.

Aisha: About forty-five minutes. We need to choose the paper and check the final colours.

Daniel: I'll send everyone a new invitation with the room number.

Aisha: Thanks. Can you put the sample list in it too? Then she can prepare her questions.

Daniel sends the invitation and removes the old one. Aisha accepts it before she starts her next task.

title: Dinner from What You Have
description: A simple cooking habit helps a household use food before buying more.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: Dinner from What You Have
units.contentMarkdown:
At six o'clock, you are hungry. You open the fridge and think, "There's nothing for dinner." But is the fridge really empty?

Before you order food, put three things on the kitchen table: something that needs cooking soon, something that will make the meal filling, and something that adds flavour.

Last Wednesday, Karim found half a cabbage and two carrots. He also had rice in the cupboard. His sister wanted to buy chicken, but the shops were busy and they were both tired.

They cut the vegetables into small pieces. Karim cooked the rice while his sister fried an onion. She added the carrots first because they were harder than the cabbage. Then she mixed everything together with a little salt and lemon juice.

The meal wasn't a special recipe. It was simply a good use of the food they already had. They saved one portion for lunch the next day.

This habit doesn't mean you must eat food you don't like or keep food that is no longer safe. Check it carefully. It means looking before shopping.

Keep a short list on your fridge: "Use these first." Write down the vegetables, opened packets and leftovers that need attention. When you go shopping, take a photo of the list.

You may still need a few ingredients. But you will have a plan, and fewer forgotten carrots at the back of the fridge.

title: The Saturday We Didn't Plan
description: Two friends discover that a changed plan can still make a good afternoon.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: The Saturday We Didn't Plan
units.contentMarkdown:
Olga and Leila planned to spend Saturday at an outdoor market. Olga wanted a plant for her room, and Leila wanted to try the food stalls. They agreed to meet outside the library at eleven.

At ten thirty, heavy rain started. Leila sent a message: "Should we stay at home?"

Olga was already on the bus. "I'm nearly there. Let's meet and decide."

When Leila arrived, Olga was standing under the library roof. Her shoes were wet, but she was laughing.

"The market can wait," she said. "What's inside here?"

They usually borrowed books from the library and left quickly. That morning, a sign near the door said: "Free board games upstairs. Everyone welcome."

Neither friend knew the rules of the game on the nearest table. A woman called Grace explained them and asked them to join. At first, Olga made several mistakes. Soon, everyone was helping each other and laughing.

After the game, they sat in the little library café. Leila drew a funny picture of Olga's wet shoes on a paper napkin.

"We didn't buy anything," Olga said.

"And we didn't spend the afternoon looking at our phones," Leila replied.

The rain stopped at three. On the way home, they passed a flower shop. Olga bought a small plant there. It cost less than the bus ticket, and she gave it a name: Saturday.

title: A Parcel for Number Twelve
description: A misplaced delivery makes a new resident rethink how she asks for help.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: A Parcel for Number Twelve
units.contentMarkdown:
The delivery app said "Handed to resident", but there was no parcel outside Mariam's door. Inside it were the shoes she needed for a job interview the following morning. She had ordered them early enough, or so she thought.

She checked the photograph attached to the message. It showed a brown box beside a green door. Her own door was white.

Mariam had moved into the building only a week before. She didn't want her first conversation with a neighbour to sound like an accusation. She walked along the corridor, looking for the door in the picture.

Number twelve was green. A man answered after her second knock.

"Sorry to bother you," she began. "I think the driver may have left my parcel here. There's a photo, but I can't see the number clearly."

The man looked behind him. "A box arrived this afternoon. My daughter orders things, so I thought it was hers. What's the name?"

Mariam told him. He picked up the box and checked the label.

"That's you. I should have looked more carefully."

She felt herself relax. "The driver probably saw twelve instead of twenty-one."

As he handed it over, he noticed the shoe shop's name. "Interview?" he asked.

"Tomorrow. How did you guess?"

"My daughter bought a pair from there before her first office job. Good luck."

Back in her flat, Mariam tried on the shoes. They fitted. She also corrected the delivery instructions in the app: third floor, white door, number twenty-one.

The next evening, she met the man by the lift. He asked how the interview had gone. She hadn't heard the result yet, but she told him about the friendly manager and the questions she had managed to answer.

The parcel problem had lasted less than an hour. Knowing someone in the building lasted longer.

title: The Deadline Is Still Friday
description: A junior colleague raises a workload problem and negotiates a realistic deadline.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: The Deadline Is Still Friday
units.contentMarkdown:
Nadia has been asked to prepare a customer report by Friday. On Wednesday, her manager adds a presentation to her task list. After checking the work remaining, Nadia asks for a short conversation.

Nadia: Can we look at my priorities? I can finish the report by Friday, but the presentation will take another full day.

Manager: I thought you could use the figures from the report. Wouldn't that make it quicker?

Nadia: The figures will help. But the presentation needs charts and a different structure. I also need to check which customer details we can share.

Manager: Fair point. The sales team wants it for Monday morning.

Nadia: Is the report needed before then too?

Manager: Yes. Finance is using it on Friday afternoon.

Nadia: Then I see two options. I could send the report on Friday and a simple presentation on Monday afternoon. Or someone could help with the charts tomorrow, and I could finish both by Friday.

Manager: What do you mean by a simple presentation?

Nadia: Six slides with the main findings. No separate examples for each region. We can add those later if the team needs them.

Manager: Monday afternoon is too late. Their meeting is at nine. I'll ask Omar whether he has time to help tomorrow.

Nadia: Thanks. If he can prepare the charts, I can write the slide text. Could you confirm the audience? That will help us choose the right details.

Manager: It's the internal sales team, including the regional managers. I'll send you the list.

Nadia: Great. I'll send Omar the checked figures by eleven tomorrow. If he's unavailable, I'll let you know before lunch so we can make another plan.

After the conversation, Nadia sends a brief message confirming who will do each task. The deadline hasn't moved, but the amount of work is now shared. She returns to the report knowing exactly what she needs to finish first.

title: A Better Way to Split the Bill
description: Friends find a fair way to share restaurant costs without an awkward argument.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: A Better Way to Split the Bill
units.contentMarkdown:
Six friends finish dinner. The food was good, the conversation was lively, and then the bill arrives. Someone suggests dividing it equally. One person goes quiet.

Equal shares are simple, but they aren't always comfortable. Perhaps one friend only had soup while another ordered three courses. Perhaps someone chose a cheap meal because they are saving for a journey. A small difference in cost can feel much larger when nobody has asked.

When Amir started a new job, his colleagues invited him to dinner. He checked the menu online and knew he could afford a main course. At the table, people ordered several shared dishes without discussing the price. He enjoyed the evening until the bill came. His share was almost twice what he had planned to spend.

He paid without saying anything. Later, he turned down two more invitations. His colleagues assumed he didn't enjoy spending time with them.

Eventually, a colleague asked him about it privately. Amir explained the problem. At the next dinner, she suggested that everyone pay for their own food and agree on shared dishes before ordering them. Nobody objected.

You don't need a complicated calculation for every meal. You do need an arrangement that people understand. Before ordering, try a neutral question: "Shall we each pay for what we have?" If everyone wants to share, ask what they would like to order and check the total together.

Restaurant staff may have limits on separate payments. Ask early rather than handing them six cards after they have printed one bill. A friend can pay the restaurant while the others send their agreed amounts, if everyone is comfortable with that.

The aim isn't to count every mouthful. It is to make sure the invitation feels like an invitation, rather than an unexpected expense.

title: One Afternoon without a Map
description: A visitor learns to ask useful questions when her phone stops working.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: One Afternoon without a Map
units.contentMarkdown:
Sofia's phone switched off just as she left the museum. She pressed the power button twice, although she knew the battery was empty. Her charger was in her hotel room. So were the paper map and the card with the hotel's address.

She remembered that the hotel was near a river, opposite a bakery. Unfortunately, she had passed several bakeries that morning.

For a moment, she considered taking a taxi. Then she realised she couldn't tell the driver where to go. She needed information before she needed transport.

Inside a bookshop, she asked whether she could charge her phone. The assistant didn't have the right cable, but he offered her a street map.

"Do you remember the name of the hotel?"

"The Riverside House. A small place with a blue sign."

He found it in a local guide and marked it on the map. It was farther away than she expected.

"You can walk along the river," he said. "It takes about forty minutes. Or take a bus from the square."

Sofia wasn't in a hurry. She bought a postcard, thanked him and chose the walk. At the square, she asked a woman which road led to the river. This time, she repeated the directions back: "Past the post office, then left at the bridge?"

"Exactly. Don't cross the bridge. Stay on this side."

Without a screen to follow, Sofia noticed details she had missed earlier: painted doors, a tiny garden between two buildings, and people carrying warm bread home. She stopped to draw the garden on the back of her postcard.

At the hotel, she plugged in her phone and wrote the address on a small piece of paper for her bag. She still wanted digital maps. She also wanted the confidence to manage when one wasn't available.

title: The Hidden Work of Being Available
description: An examination of response-time expectations and boundaries in a small team.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: The Hidden Work of Being Available
units.contentMarkdown:
At 8:47 on a Sunday evening, Elena's phone lit up. Her manager had sent a short message: "Could you check the figures before tomorrow? No rush." Elena was watching a film with her brother. She put the phone face down, then picked it up again three minutes later.

The words said that the task could wait. The timing suggested something else. If she ignored it, would she seem unreliable? If she answered, would Sunday evening become a normal time to work?

Availability can look like a personal habit, but it is often a team agreement that nobody has actually made. One colleague sends messages whenever an idea occurs to him, intending others to read them later. Another interprets every notification as a request for immediate action. Both believe they are being considerate, yet one person's convenience creates another person's interruption.

In Elena's team, the problem became visible when a new employee asked which channel to use for urgent issues. There was no clear answer. Routine questions arrived in the same chat as genuine emergencies, and the most responsive person usually dealt with both.

The team tried a modest change. Ordinary messages could still be written at any time, but replies were expected during working hours. Anything needed earlier had to include a clear deadline. Problems that genuinely couldn't wait required a phone call, along with an explanation of why waiting would cause harm.

The arrangement wasn't perfect. The first week, Elena still checked her phone automatically. Her manager also had to change his behaviour: he scheduled non-urgent messages for the following morning instead of sending them late at night. Gradually, silence outside work stopped looking like a lack of commitment.

There are jobs where someone must be available after hours. In those cases, the useful questions are who is responsible, for how long, and how that responsibility is recognised. An unwritten expectation that everyone should always be reachable answers none of them.

A boundary is more convincing when it describes what will happen, rather than merely asking people to be respectful. "We value your free time" sounds reassuring. "Messages sent after six will normally receive a reply the next working day" gives people something they can act on.

Elena finished the film that Sunday. On Monday morning, she checked the figures. The work was completed, and her brother didn't have to compete with a spreadsheet for the rest of the evening.

title: The Cheapest Room in the City
description: A traveller weighs a cheap booking against hidden costs and learns to ask precise questions.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: The Cheapest Room in the City
units.contentMarkdown:
The room looked almost suspiciously affordable. It had a desk, a private bathroom and a window overlooking a quiet courtyard. For Karim, who was attending a two-day training course, it seemed ideal. The listing said "twenty minutes from the centre". He booked before the last discounted room disappeared.

Only after the confirmation arrived did he check the address properly. Twenty minutes meant twenty minutes by car in light traffic. By public transport, the journey involved two buses and a long walk. His course began at eight thirty, and the first bus wouldn't get him there in time.

He contacted the host. His first draft sounded angry: "Your description is misleading. I want a refund." Before sending it, he read the cancellation conditions again. The room was non-refundable, and the description hadn't actually claimed that the journey was possible by bus.

He rewrote the message. He explained his course times, asked whether there was an earlier transport option, and said that the location would make his stay difficult. Could the host offer a partial refund if the room was booked by someone else?

The host replied that evening. There was a shared taxi used by local workers, but its route changed according to demand. She couldn't promise when it would arrive. However, she was willing to release the room for another booking. If it sold, she would refund the room charge, keeping the booking fee.

Karim had to decide whether to risk paying for two rooms. He calculated the likely taxi fares, the time spent travelling and the cost of a hotel within walking distance of the course. The central hotel was more expensive per night, but the total difference was smaller than he had assumed.

He chose it. The original room was eventually booked for one of the two nights, so he recovered part of the cost. It wasn't the bargain he had hoped for, but it was manageable.

At the course, another participant praised the same cheap listing. Karim didn't tell her to avoid it. She was travelling by car and visiting family nearby; for her, the location made sense.

He showed her the map instead. "Ask what the travel time includes," he said. "The room may be cheap. Getting to the place you need can be the expensive part."

title: An Apology with a Next Step
description: Two colleagues repair trust after a private conversation is repeated to a group.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: An Apology with a Next Step
units.contentMarkdown:
During a team lunch, Tom repeats something Salma told him privately: she is considering applying for another job. She changes the subject, but later asks to speak to him alone.

Salma: I want to talk about what you said at lunch. I hadn't told the team I was looking elsewhere. Now my manager may hear about it before I've even decided to apply.

Tom: I'm sorry. I thought you were just discussing possibilities. I didn't realise it was confidential.

Salma: I understand that I didn't use the word "confidential". But it was a conversation between us, and I didn't give you permission to pass it on.

Tom: You're right. I should have asked. I put you in a difficult position.

Salma: Yes. And when you laughed about me "escaping", it made it sound as if I dislike the team. That isn't what I said.

Tom: I was trying to make a joke, but I can see how it sounded. Would it help if I sent everyone a message explaining that?

Salma: Please don't send anything yet. A group message might draw more attention to it. I need time to think about what I want my manager to know.

Tom: All right. What would you like me to do if someone asks about it?

Salma: Say that you shouldn't have spoken for me and that they should ask me directly. Don't add more details, even if you think they'll make things better.

Tom: I can do that. And I'll check with you before repeating anything personal in future.

Salma: Thank you. I'm still upset. I don't want you to take that as a sign that I haven't heard your apology.

Tom: I won't. You don't have to make me feel better about it.

The following day, a colleague asks Tom whether Salma has accepted another position. He gives the answer they agreed on. He doesn't tell Salma immediately and expect praise; he simply keeps the boundary.

For Salma, the apology matters, but the next few weeks matter more. Trust will depend on whether Tom's behaviour changes when there is no uncomfortable conversation reminding him to be careful.

title: When a Family Recipe Travels
description: A family disagreement over an ingredient explores memory, adaptation and belonging.
author: OmniClass · Original readings
attribution: Original English text written for OmniClass with OpenAI Codex, October 2026. No third-party source text.

units.title: When a Family Recipe Travels
units.contentMarkdown:
When Rania sent her mother a photograph of dinner, she expected a heart emoji. Instead, the reply came almost immediately: "What have you put in the filling?"

Rania was living abroad and had made the stuffed vegetables she remembered from home. The familiar herbs were difficult to find near her flat, so she had used a different mixture. She had also cooked them in a wide frying pan because she didn't own a large pot. Her mother recognised the dish, but not quite the version on the screen.

Food often carries instructions that are never written down. A recipe may list the ingredients, yet leave out how tightly to pack the vegetables, when to lower the heat, or what "a little" salt means. These details are learnt by watching someone whose movements seem too ordinary to explain.

Distance changes that process. Rania couldn't stand beside her mother at the cooker. Instead, they exchanged photographs and voice messages. Her mother told her to listen for the sound of the liquid bubbling and showed her how to judge when the filling was ready. Rania explained the ingredients available in her neighbourhood and the equipment she could afford.

At first, each treated the differences as mistakes. Her mother worried that the family dish was becoming something else. Rania felt that every substitution was being judged as a failure to remember home properly. Neither was really arguing about herbs alone.

Their conversations became easier when they separated two questions: what creates the dish's characteristic flavour, and what can change without losing the pleasure of eating it? Some choices mattered to both of them. Others turned out to be habits rather than necessities.

A month later, Rania invited friends for dinner. She described the food as her version of a family recipe and explained the changes without apologising for them. One guest asked for written instructions. Rania made two columns in her notebook: "What my mother uses" and "What I can find here".

She sent the page home. This time, her mother replied with a photograph of her own dinner. She had tried Rania's method in the frying pan because it was easier to wash.

A recipe can preserve a connection without preserving every movement unchanged. In this family, the conversation around the dish became part of what was passed on.
